subject: DBMS
original_question: सख्त 2PL (Strict Two-Phase Locking) कैस्केडिंग रोलबैक को कैसे रोकता है?
translated_question: How does Strict Two-Phase Locking prevent cascading rollback?

retrieved_chunks_details.subject: dbms
retrieved_chunks_details.text: Two-Phase Locking (2PL) and Serializability Serializability is the standard criterion for the correctness of concurrent transaction execution. A concurrent schedule is conflict serializable if it is conflict equivalent to some serial schedule, which can be verified by constructing a precedence (or serialization) graph: a schedule is conflict serializable if and only if its precedence graph has no directed cycles. The Two-Phase Locking (2PL) protocol is a concurrency control mechanism that guarantees conflict serializability. Under basic 2PL: - Growing Phase: A transaction may acquire locks (shared or exclusive), but cannot release any lock. - Shrinking Phase: A transaction may release locks, but cannot acquire any new lock. Strict 2PL further requires that all exclusive locks held by a transaction be released only after the transaction commits or aborts, which prevents cascading rollbacks. Rigorous 2PL requires both shared and exclusive locks to be held until commit.

retrieved_chunks_details.text: Database Management Systems: ACID Transactions and Concurrency Control A transaction in a database management system is a logical unit of database processing that includes one or more database access operations. Transactions must satisfy the ACID properties: 1. Atomicity: Either all operations of the transaction are executed and reflected in the database, or none are. Handled by the write-ahead logging (WAL) recovery manager. 2. Consistency: Execution of a transaction in isolation preserves database consistency invariants and integrity constraints. 3. Isolation: Even if multiple transactions execute concurrently, the system guarantees that for every pair of transactions T_i and T_j, it appears to T_i that either T_j finished execution before T_i started, or T_j started execution after T_i finished. 4. Durability: Once a transaction successfully commits, the updates made to the database persist even in the event of system crashes.

retrieved_chunks_details.text: Operating Systems: Process Synchronization and Deadlocks In multiprogramming environments, concurrent access to shared data can lead to data inconsistency. A race condition arises when several processes access and manipulate the same data concurrently and the outcome depends on the particular order in which access takes place. The critical-section problem requires three structural conditions to be satisfied: 1. Mutual Exclusion: If process P_i is executing in its critical section, then no other processes can be executing in their critical sections. 2. Progress: If no process is executing in its critical section and there exist some processes that wish to enter their critical section, then only those processes not executing in their remainder sections can participate in deciding which will enter next. 3. Bounded Waiting: There must be a bound on the number of times other processes are allowed to enter their critical sections after a process has made a request to enter and before that request is granted.

retrieved_chunks_details.text: Coffman's Four Conditions for Deadlock A deadlock is a state in which each process in a set is waiting for an event that only another process in the set can cause. Edward G. Coffman Jr. formalized that a deadlock situation can arise if and only if all four of the following conditions hold simultaneously: 1. Mutual Exclusion: At least one resource must be held in a non-shareable mode (only one process can use the resource at a time). 2. Hold and Wait: A process must be currently holding at least one resource and requesting additional resources that are currently being held by other processes. 3. No Preemption: Resources cannot be forcibly preempted from a process; a resource can only be released voluntarily by the process holding it after completing its task. 4. Circular Wait: A closed chain of processes exists such that each process holds at least one resource needed by the next process in the chain (P_0 waits for resource held by P_1, ..., P_n waits for resource held by P_0).

retrieved_chunks_details.text: TCP Flow Control vs Congestion Control It is vital to distinguish between flow control and congestion control in computer networks: - Flow Control is a speed-matching service that prevents a fast sender from overwhelming a slow receiver's buffer space. TCP implements flow control using a receive window (`rwnd`) field in the TCP header. The receiver explicitly informs the sender of how many spare bytes of buffer space are currently available (`rwnd = RcvBuffer - [LastByteRcvd - LastByteRead]`). The sender ensures that the unacknowledged data never exceeds `rwnd`. - Congestion Control prevents senders from injecting too much traffic into the network subnet, avoiding packet loss and queue collapse in intermediate routers. TCP maintains a congestion window (`cwnd`). The effective transmission window is $\min(\text{cwnd}, \text{rwnd})$. TCP congestion control algorithms (such as TCP Reno and Tahoe) employ four phases: Slow Start (exponential window growth), Congestion Avoidance (additive increase / multiplicative decrease, AIMD), Fast Retransmit, and Fast Recovery.
